extracted.intended_audience: Los Angeles readers interested in comedy, improv fans, and potential festival-goers
extracted.subtask_description: A local-news preview/feature about a longform improv festival (UCB Del Close Marathon) moving to Los Angeles, describing format, highlights, audience differences, and logistics. Useful for readers deciding what to see and performers/organizers planning participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of longform improvisation
rubrics_metrics.description: "The form of comedy, made up in scenes based on suggestions from the audience, that the Upright Citizens Brigade has been teaching and performing for decades."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames DCM as a celebration of longform improv (as opposed to short-form games); implies evaluation should consider scene-based, suggestion-driven storytelling rather than set sketches or prepared material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience sensibility differences (L.A. vs New York)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements that New York audiences tend to be younger/college-aged and more willing to laugh at someone 'having something bad happen' onstage; L.A. audiences are 'hipper, and a little older' and 'more sensitive... maybe more sympathetic' and may look around to see if others are laughing first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication for performers: adjust tone and stakes for the local audience—NY crowds may reward edgier, shock, or abrasive bits, while L.A. crowds may respond better to sympathetic, emotionally grounded choices. Quoted lines: Moynihan on NY vs L.A. audience behavior; Appel on sensitivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of successful live improv performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Performers should 'find another new thing that's interesting' and value the shared, unified experience where 'the room becomes unified in a very wonderful and beautiful way.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative criteria include novelty (continually finding new choices), audience buy-in/ensemble connection, and emotional clarity. Walsh emphasizes challenge and discomfort in front of live audiences as a mark of meaningful performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overnight marathon show characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Overnight portions are described as 'the craziest shows' featuring 'big crazy ideas in short bursts' where 'it usually gets rowdy,' with chairs thrown and cups of beer whipped at faces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These sets should be judged on energy, unpredictability, and boundary-pushing spectacle rather than polish or star power. The article notes physical stunts, messy/gnarly elements, and extreme improvisational bits as trademarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Festival scale and logistics
rubrics_metrics.description: This year's move allows a smaller scale in L.A.: fewer teams from around the country, reduced number of venues (kept to three stages at UCB's Franklin and Sunset locations), and different transit/logistics considerations in L.A. (encouraging Lyft rather than walking/subway).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizational criteria include venue concentration, manageability, and local transportation realities. The shift to smaller scale is framed as intentional and practical for rebuilding the festival in a new city.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ticketing model and audience access
rubrics_metrics.description: Shifted to more of an à la carte model: selling tickets to certain blocks of shows rather than all-access wristbands; this means less comedy in one go but avoids giant lines that were a hallmark in New York.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should consider trade-offs between comprehensiveness (all-access) and attendee convenience (smaller queues, targeted attendance). Passes for overnight shows allow come-and-go flexibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local vs touring talent selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Part of the shift includes focusing on UCB's own homegrown talent and bringing in fewer teams from around the country; many performers now live in L.A., removing need to fly them out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curatorial criteria: prioritize local/homegrown acts for sustainability and founder participation; impacts festival character and ability of founders to appear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show types and creative formats to highlight
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of recommended/featured formats: Buffoons (sketch + one-act play + memorial service + performance art), improvised musicals, Blindfolded improv, improvised commentary with fake cast/crew, Shamilton (improvised Hamilton style), and shows that incorporate multimedia (e.g., screening an Ozark episode as part of a set).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criteria for standout shows include hybridity (mixing forms), unpredictability, meta-humor, musicality, risk-taking (blindfolds, stunts), and willingness to experiment with media and formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of the marathon for performer development and community
rubrics_metrics.description: DCM functions as a place where many star improvisers started as students; it's described as 'a ladder, a stepping stone to get better at it,' and a place to 'be part of developing those people's voices.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess festival success partly by its role in talent development, teaching opportunities, and the extent to which it nurtures a pipeline from students to professional careers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity and inclusion as a value
rubrics_metrics.description: Walsh notes being 'happy to see the improv artform diversifying beyond largely white men' and proud of DCM's role in 'turn[ing] people on to improv and comedy' as an outlet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply inclusion metrics: diversity of performers and perspectives, opportunities for underrepresented groups, and whether programming expands access and representation in improv.

rubrics_metrics.name: Programming that rewards risk and spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples cited include Rob Riggle ripping seats off chairs and wrestling, Anthony Atamanuik performing on a stage covered with whipped cream despite injuring his back, and shows like 'We're Playing Britney Spears' Toxic for Ten Minutes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate certain acts on boldness, willingness to risk physical comedy or elaborate bits, and ability to create memorable, headline-making moments—particularly in marathon/overnight contexts where spectacle is prized.
